concepts.title: Space radiation
concepts.lead: Invisible, energetic particles reach Mars. A radiation rate describes how quickly their energy is absorbed.
concepts.analogy: Think of invisible rain: a detector counts what arrives, while a shelter changes how much gets through.
concepts.explanation: Real space radiation varies. Our mission starts from a historical Mars detector value, then uses an authored rising-rate curve for the story. The NASA Sun image is a separate observation; it does not set this mission's storm or radiation rate.
concepts.equation: Story rate = 210 × (1 + 3 × elapsed / mission time) µGy/day
concepts.real_fact: Curiosity's RAD measured radiation at Gale Crater during 2012–2013. These historical observations are not today's Mars weather.
concepts.assumption: The rise from 210 to 840 µGy/day over 30 mission minutes is invented for this lesson. It is not a NASA storm prediction, personal dose rate, or safety threshold.
concepts.dynamic_hint: The story rate rises with mission time. Changing the cleaning pace does not change radiation arriving each second.

concepts.title: Tiny energy
concepts.lead: A gray measures radiation energy absorbed per kilogram. A microgray is one millionth of a gray.
concepts.analogy: A bucket collects raindrops over time. Dose also adds up, but measures absorbed energy, not water or damage.
concepts.explanation: Our µGy counter adds absorbed model dose over time. When the radiation rate changes, we add rate × each small time step. Curiosity measured a historical average of 210 µGy per Earth day at Gale Crater; this game counter is not a measurement of Ren or a real person.
concepts.equation: Dose = sum of changing rate × each time step
concepts.real_fact: Hassler and colleagues reported 210 ± 40 µGy/day in RAD's tissue-like E detector at Gale Crater, August 2012–June 2013.
concepts.source_label: NASA research archive: Hassler et al.
concepts.assumption: Every complete 30-minute run receives 10.9375 µGy under the same authored curve. Pauses do not spend mission time. There are no lower-dose bonus stars.
concepts.dynamic_hint: All complete runs have the same outside duration and dose curve. Pace changes cleaning, not the final dose.

concepts.title: Meet sievert
concepts.lead: Sievert describes weighted radiation quantities. We need more information than absorbed dose to calculate it.
concepts.analogy: The same amount of rain can affect a leaf and a roof differently. The amount alone does not explain every effect.
concepts.explanation: Gray measures absorbed energy per kilogram. Radiation type weighting is needed for equivalent dose; effective dose also uses tissue weighting. Our model lacks those inputs, so it cannot calculate Sv from its µGy counter. A smartwatch does not supply the missing space-radiation measurements.
concepts.equation: Sv calculation needs radiation and tissue weighting
concepts.real_fact: EPA defines 1 gray as 1 joule per kilogram. Effective dose adjusts absorbed dose for radiation type and relative organ sensitivity.
concepts.assumption: The Sievert bubble is a learning card. It shows no invented personal Sv value, medical risk, or health score.
concepts.dynamic_hint: Needs radiation/tissue weighting. A µGy reading alone cannot produce a personal sievert estimate.

concepts.title: Dusty panels
concepts.lead: Dust blocks some sunlight from a solar panel. Cleaning a section can help more light reach its cells.
concepts.analogy: A dusty window lets less light into a room. Clearing it helps the light come through again.
concepts.explanation: Dust reduces the light reaching solar cells. Ren starts brushing only after START MISSION. Every partial section counts as cleaning. Removing dust raises available solar power, which can charge the battery after the dome uses what it needs.
concepts.equation: Clean fraction = cleaned sections ÷ total sections
concepts.real_fact: A NASA paper reports a 0.28% per day decrease in short-circuit current from Pathfinder's dust experiment. That is one historical result, not a universal dust rate.
concepts.assumption: The array has 4 modeled sections. Light transmission rises linearly from 25% when dirty to 100% when fully clean. These are authored values, not measured hardware performance.
concepts.dynamic_hint: Dust remaining is 100% minus the cleaned fraction. The battery gains energy over time as solar generation exceeds the dome load.

concepts.title: Stored energy
concepts.lead: Solar panels supply power. The battery stores energy left after the habitat's needs are met.
concepts.analogy: A tap fills a tank while another pipe drains it. The tank's stored water changes according to the difference.
concepts.explanation: kW measures how fast energy flows. kWh measures energy stored in the battery. We add solar energy made during each time step, subtract energy supplied to the dome, and respect the battery capacity. The result shows actual simulated energy at mission end.
concepts.real_fact: Mars Exploration Rover power models tracked solar generation, loads, and batteries, with dust, temperature, shadows, and other environmental inputs.
concepts.assumption: The clear-array 8 kW rating,1 kW dome load,0.5 kWh starting energy and 6 kWh battery capacity are fictional lesson settings. WIN/PASS/LOSE comes from the cleaned fraction.
concepts.dynamic_hint: Stored now is actual simulated battery energy. A high kW reading is a rate, not energy already saved.

concepts.title: Mission time
concepts.lead: The countdown gives Ren 30 mission minutes to clean. When it ends, she steps straight into shelter.
concepts.analogy: Like a timed art activity, you choose a comfortable pace until the bell rings. Pauses for learning stop the clock.
concepts.explanation: At standard play speed, one real second advances six mission seconds. Nothing advances before START MISSION. Reading cards and taking a break pause the clock. Every completed round has the same outside duration; there is no walk or recall button.
concepts.equation: Time remaining = mission duration − elapsed time
concepts.real_fact: NASA describes a Martian sol as approximately 24.6 Earth hours. Our radiation conversion uses an Earth day of 86,400 seconds, not a sol.
concepts.assumption: The 30-minute mission, accelerated clock and automatic shelter entry are story choices. The radiation conversion uses an Earth day of 86,400 seconds, not a Martian sol.
concepts.dynamic_hint: Mission Time and this bubble share one clock. When the countdown reaches zero, Ren enters immediately and the result appears.

concepts.title: Pace and tiredness
concepts.lead: Faster work can tire Ren. A tired Ren cleans more slowly, so pace needs balance.
concepts.analogy: Imagine wiping a table: rushing hard can tire your arm. Easing up gives it a chance to recover.
concepts.explanation: The pace slider sets a command multiplier from 0.25× to 1.75×. Commands above 1× build modeled tiredness; commands below 1× reduce it. Effective cleaning rate depends on both the command and current tiredness. These are invented game rules, not a fitness or medical model.
concepts.real_fact: NASA's Pathfinder dust experiment measured how settled dust reduced solar-cell output. It did not measure an astronaut's cleaning rate.
concepts.assumption: Tiredness stays between 0 and 0.9. Per mission minute it changes by 0.08×max(pace−1,0)−0.12×max(1−pace,0). These coefficients are authored and are not NASA human-performance data.
concepts.dynamic_hint: The command is not the same as effective cleaning rate. Faster and slower change pace; tiredness builds or recovers over mission time.

concepts.title: A step inside
concepts.lead: Ren is already beside the shelter door. At zero on the countdown, she steps straight inside.
concepts.analogy: Like standing beside a doorway while doing a task, coming inside does not require a journey across the yard.
concepts.explanation: Rock, soil and habitat walls can change the radiation that reaches an astronaut. Some energetic particles still get through. Our cleaning round ends at the deadline and Ren enters immediately. The model stops there; it does not claim indoor radiation becomes zero.
concepts.equation: Countdown reaches zero → immediate shelter entry
concepts.real_fact: In September 2016, Curiosity measured about 4% less overall radiation beside Murray Buttes. This observation does not certify any habitat design.
concepts.assumption: There is no walk, distance-driven travel, entry delay or recall decision in this mission. Shelter is fixed beside Ren. This does not simulate pressure cycling or certify a real habitat.
concepts.dynamic_hint: Automatic entry ends the full-length round. The outcome is based on the fraction cleaned, not a made-up dose bonus.
